Many in your position learn to recognize that particular gaze—not as truth, but as a symptom of a community that has itself been traumatized into scarcity thinking, where belonging is guarded like a dwindling resource. You do not have to answer that sentence. You can let it hang in the air, unanswered, and turn back to the conversation you were actually having.

**They build parallel rooms.**  
There are more of you than it seems. Urban Sámi, reclaimed Sámi, language-less Sámi, Sámi who grew up in Oslo because their parents or grandparents were moved, shamed, or separated from their communities. People in this liminal space often find each other—not to replace the broader community, but to stop the isolation. These networks might look like art collectives, online spaces, urban associations, or simply small friendships with others who understand what it means to be “not quite enough for one side and too much for the other.” In those rooms, you are not a guest. You are a host.

It is fair—necessary, even—to set boundaries that protect you. *“I can’t speak for all Sámi people,”* or *“That’s outside my experience,”* or simply *“I don’t know.”* You do not owe your workplace a polished cultural performance any more than you owe the woman at the gathering a flawless bloodline recitation.

**They practice culture as relationship, not credential.**  
Some learn the language, if they choose to, not to prove anything but to speak to the land and to ancestors. Others take up duodji, cook with traditional foods, listen to joik, or simply think in the ways they were raised. None of this is a resume. You are tired because you are being asked to solve, with your individual body, a structural problem that required generations to create. It is what kind of Sámi life you are willing to build—quietly, stubbornly, without apology—in a city that once tried to make you forget you had a home at all.

I am sorry you are carrying this. The drawing on the refrigerator is a kind of love, and it is crushing to feel you cannot promise her what she has drawn.

With a six-year-old, the goal is not to explain immigration policy or existential uncertainty. It is to separate the *building* from the *belonging*. She needs to know that one can be uncertain while the other is absolute.

Here is a way to approach it, using language that matches how a child that age thinks.

**Start with what she already knows.**
Hold the picture with her.  
*“I love this. You are right—this is our home. Home is where your bed is, where we eat pancakes on Sundays, where you put your stickers, and where your drawing lives on the refrigerator.”*

**Introduce the idea that “home” can move, because the family is the part that stays.**
*“But here is a secret about home: it can travel. Home is not just the walls. It is us. It is you and me. So even if one day we lived in a different building, in a different city, we would still be home, because we would still be us.”*

**Name the uncertainty without placing it on her.**
*“Right now there are some grown-up rules—like big, confusing homework that even I don’t get to grade—that might mean we cannot stay in this exact apartment forever. I don’t know yet what will happen. But I do know this: I promise you will always have a home. I promise you will always be with me. I promise we will be safe together.”*

**Let her ask concrete questions.**
At six, her fears will be physical and immediate: *Will I bring my stuffed animal? Will I go to a new school? Will you be there?* Answer only what she asks, simply and truthfully.  
*“Yes, your bunny would come. Yes, I would be with you. I don’t know about the school yet, but we would figure it out together.”*

**Avoid the abstract phrase “home is not something you can promise.”**
That is a truth for adults, but for a six-year-old it sounds like *I cannot promise you safety.* Instead, let her hear that the *place* may change, but the *home*—the promise of her place in your family—does not.

**One more thing:** If no decision has been made and no move is imminent, you do not need to have this conversation today unless she is asking. Children sense stress, but they also benefit from ordinary routines. It is okay to let her simply be six while the review is open, and to carry the uncertainty for her until there is something concrete to name.

You are not betraying her by loving that picture and also knowing it might not last. You are teaching her that home is something you build together, not just something you receive. That is a hard lesson, but it is also a true one, and she will learn it from the steadiness in your voice when you say, *“Wherever we are, we are home.”*

Here is the most realistic path when you have $0 and no one waiting for you.

**1. Do not move for an apartment. Move for a bed that comes with a paycheck.**
The only reliable way to land in a city with no savings and no network is to secure housing *through* employment before you arrive. Apply for jobs that include room and board:
- Residential caregiving (group homes, assisted living, overnight shifts often let you sleep on-site between rounds)
- Live-in nanny or elder companion
- Seasonal resort or hotel staff (housekeeping, kitchen, maintenance; many provide dorm-style housing)
- National parks, summer camps, or cruise ships
- Farm work with housing (harvest labor, horse stables)

These jobs usually hire quickly and care less about a local address. They get you inside the city limits, earning, so you can look for the next thing without paying rent out of pocket.

**2. If you already have a job in town, stay put for 6–8 weeks and build a “stupid, tiny fund.”**
If you are employed right now, the fastest escape is often a delayed one. Stop spending. Sell the car if you can use transit/buses to commute, or keep it but sleep in it later. Plasma, overtime, whatever. You need roughly $800–$1,200. That buys you 10–14 days in a cheap hostel or motel while you hit the pavement in person. Do not try to rent an apartment remotely with no savings; you will lose deposits to scams or simply get ignored.

**3. Stop applying online. Arrive and walk in.**
The three jobs you applied to from afar went nowhere because cities are full of local applicants who can interview tomorrow. Once you are in the city:
- Day 1: Register with every temp agency (warehouse, event setup, data entry, construction cleanup). Many will put you to work the next morning.
- Day 2: Walk into restaurants, grocery stores, and hotels with a paper resume and ask for the manager. Food service and dishwashing turn over constantly; they often need a body more than a credential.
- Gig apps (delivery, TaskRabbit) can start within days if you have a phone and a bike or car.

**4. Use the church infrastructure you already know.**
You mentioned your mother’s friends at church. Whether or not you believe anymore, that system is a logistics network. Call a congregation of your denomination in your target city. Ask for the pastor or the deacon who handles “transitions” or “benevolence.” Explain literally: *I am relocating with very little money and need to know if anyone has a room for rent or a lead on a job.* Churches often have basement apartments, parishioners with empty nests, and funds for exactly this kind of arrival. It is far more effective than Craigslist because it comes with a pre-vouched social contract.

**5. The car is either your shelter or your ticket in.**
If you own the car you drive past the mayor’s sign in, you have an asset. The math is grim but real: people do sleep in their cars for 2–4 weeks while working a new city job, showering at a cheap gym or truck stop, until they can pay a deposit on a room. If the car is reliable, this is an option. If it is not, sell it for the stupid, tiny fund.

**6. Ask your cousin for the spreadsheet, not the postcard.**
Call your cousin and ask specific, unromantic questions: *What did you do the first week? How much did it actually cost? Who did you know?* If she is in Berlin and you are trying to move to a domestic city, ask if she knows anyone there—an old classmate, a former coworker, someone she met online. Weak ties are how most people actually move. The “air” in her voice is useful data; it means survival is possible.

**7. Your first housing will not be an apartment.**
It will be a sublet, a room in a shared house, or a month-to-month situation found through city-specific Facebook groups or Reddit housing threads. Look for listings where someone needs a roommate immediately and is willing to take a deposit in installments after your first paycheck. Do not look for your own place. Look for a corner in someone else’s.

**A specific first step:**
If you are serious within the next 30 days, pick one city. Find three live-in or residential-care jobs in that city. Call their hiring managers directly (do not just email) and say: *“I am relocating and available to start immediately. Do you provide staff housing during training?”* If one says yes, you have a door.

The city will not fix the part of you that feels over-known. That loneliness will follow you, and the city will add a new loneliness on top of it. But the air in your cousin’s voice is the sound of a life that is still being decided. You can decide yours too. You just have to arrive with a bed attached to a job, or you will be deciding it from the backseat of your car—which is also a decision, and not always a bad one, but it helps to know which one you are making.

For the job application, put your aunt’s address. It is the address where you are staying, it is where you can receive mail, and it is the truth. Employers mostly need an address for payroll taxes, W-2s, and background paperwork; they are not evaluating whether the house is overcrowded. If you can get mail there and sleep there, it counts.

If your aunt’s place truly cannot receive mail for you (or if you are worried about it being rejected), these are the safer alternatives:

*   **General Delivery** at your local post office. You will need to ask the clerk for the proper format; it usually looks like “General Delivery, [City], [State], [Zip].” Some online forms reject this, but it is a real, legal address.
*   **In care of** a trusted friend or family member who has a stable address and will hand you your mail immediately.
*   **A reentry organization, church, or social service agency** that allows people to use their address for mail. Many reentry programs specifically offer this.

Do not make up an address. If a background check later contradicts it, that is an automatic “no” from most employers.

Now, the harder part: your parole officer and your check-in.

**You need to separate the job address from the parole address in your head.** Using your aunt’s address for a paycheck does not fix the fact that your PO says it is not a “stable residence.” That is a housing crisis, not a job-application crisis. You must deal with it before check-in, or you risk a violation.

Call your PO **today** or **tomorrow** and tell them the truth: you applied to four places, two ghosted you, two rejected you after the background check, and you are still at your aunt’s. Ask them directly:
*   “Do you have an emergency bed list or a transitional housing referral?”
*   “Can a shelter or halfway house count as stable for now?”
*   “If my aunt writes a letter saying I am staying here and I start paying a small amount toward utilities, does that make this address acceptable?”

Many POs have a list of reentry housing they never mention unless you ask. Some will accept a shelter or even a verified room in an overcrowded house if there is paperwork backing it up.

Also call **211** (in the U.S.) and ask specifically for “reentry housing” or “ex-offender transitional housing.” Ask for reentry nonprofits in your county. If you are near a major city, there are almost always organizations that exist solely to help people in your exact spot.

**For Thursday’s interview:**

If they ask about your address, say something short and professional:  
*“I’m staying with family right now while I’m getting into my own place. I’m reliable, I have a phone, and I can be here on time.”*

Do not volunteer that you were incarcerated unless you are legally required to or unless the application specifically asks. If they run a background check and it comes up, be ready with one calm sentence: *“I made mistakes in the past, I served my time, and I’m here to work.”* Then stop talking.

The most important thing right now is that **you do not let the housing problem cost you the job**. A paycheck is what gets you into a stable address that your PO will accept. Put the aunt’s address on the form, get through Thursday, and keep making calls about housing today so you have something to tell your PO at check-in.

You can do both at once: apply for the job honestly, and fight for the housing urgently.

You do not go back. You arrive.

What was taken from you cannot be retrieved like a toy left behind a couch. That child who knew the language in their body, who heard it in the cadence of love and anger and lullabies, lived in a different world than the one you were moved into. The house that spoke only English was doing what such houses often do: it was making you legible to a power that did not want you to remain whole. That is not your shame to carry. It is a violence done to you, and the part of you that still aches for those words is proof that you survived it.

Your nana held your face in her hands and said nothing. That silence was not failure. That was a conversation. Her hands were speaking. Her eyes were speaking. The grief in the room was speaking. You understood more than you think you did. You understood that you had lost a bridge, and that she had lost you on the other side of it, and that both of you were standing there wishing the bridge were still there. That is a kind of understanding that runs deeper than vocabulary.

The app cannot know this because an app is a tool, not a memory. It teaches a standardized, flattened language—useful, but bloodless. It does not know the particular way your nana says *granddaughter*, or the word she uses for the specific pot she cooks in, or the phrase she mutters when she is worried about rain. It does not know the intonation that means *I am scolding you because I am afraid for you*, or the one that means *I have waited so long to touch your face*. These are not in the curriculum. They live only in bodies and in relationships.

So how do you return to it?

You stop trying to become the child you were, and you start becoming the adult who learns it as an act of love. This will look different. It will be slower. It will be humbling. You will sit with your nana—not at a family gathering where the noise and shame are too loud, but alone, if you can—and ask her for five words. Not “useful” words. *Her* words. The words for *forehead*, *tongue*, *hunger*, *home*. Record her voice on your phone. Let her hear her own voice played back. Let her laugh at your bad pronunciation. Let her correct you. The correction is a gift; it means she believes you are worth teaching.

You will not become a native speaker. That door closed when you were small, and grieving that is part of the work. But you can become something else: a living bridge. You can carry enough of it forward that, if you have children, they will know that their grandmother had a tongue that tasted like something specific, and that their parent fought to hear it again. You can learn enough to say, at the end, the things that need to be said while she can still hear them.

The language was taken, but it was not erased. Some of it is still in your ear, in the way you hear music, in your dreams. Some of it is waiting in her hands. Go to her not as the child who lost it, but as the thirty-four-year-old who is strong enough to be a beginner, strong enough to sit in the silence until the words come back—not perfectly, not completely, but enough.

Enough to hold her face in *your* hands, and say something. Even if it is small. Even if it is broken. She will hear it.

I’m sorry you are in this situation. Needing to take a young child on a long water journey before dawn is hard, and the fact that you are weighing her safety against her need to learn the route tells me you are already trying to protect her.

**If her neck is “doing something it didn’t used to do,” the safest choice is to stop putting weight on her head now.** That symptom—clicking, catching, grinding, or shifting—means the load is already altering how her cervical spine or shoulder girdle is moving. At seven, her growth plates are still open, her neck muscles are still developing the endurance to hold a lordotic curve under load, and her head-to-body ratio is larger than an adult’s. Carrying water on the head places the entire load through the cervical spine and compresses the soft discs. If a load is heavy enough to change how her neck moves, it can damage ligaments or vertebrae while she is still growing, and that damage can become permanent.

Here is how to handle both the immediate risk and the need for her to learn the way.

### What to do about the carrying

**1. Remove the head load immediately.**
Do not let her carry water on her head again until she has seen a health worker if at all possible, and certainly not until her neck has been symptom-free for a long time. A seven-year-old should not be carrying heavy water loads on her head. If water *must* be carried by children, the weight should be distributed through the shoulders and hips (like a small backpack), and even then it should be very light—generally no more than **10 percent of her body weight**, and less if she is walking a long distance over uneven ground.

**2. She can learn the route without carrying the burden.**
“Knowing the way” is about landmarks, turns, pace, and safety—not about hauling water. She can walk beside you with:
- An empty small container (so she practices balance without weight),
- A light cloth sack with a little food or a change of clothes,
- Or nothing at all, simply observing and memorizing.

If she must help transport water, use methods that spare her neck and spine:
- **Divide the water.** Several very small containers carried in both hands at her sides, switching hands frequently, so no single side bears the load.
- **A pole or yoke** across the shoulders with small buckets or bottles hanging from each end, if materials are available. This keeps weight off the neck and skull.
- **A small backpack or cloth sack** on her back, not her head, with only a liter or two if she is strong enough.
- **Rolling, if terrain allows.** A sturdy container rolled along the path keeps weight off her body entirely.

### If head-loading is unavoidable for anyone in your group (harm reduction)

In many places, head-loading is a necessity. If an adult or older adolescent must do it and you need to teach her only for emergency knowledge (not daily practice at age seven), these are the principles that reduce harm:

- **Use a head pad or ring.** A firm, rounded pad (woven grass, cloth, rubber, or wood) that sits on the crown of the head, not the forehead or back of skull. It keeps the neck in a neutral position.
- **Center the load.** The container must sit balanced so she does not tilt or twist her neck to keep it on. Any imbalance multiplies strain.
- **Keep the neck straight.** The chin should be slightly tucked, eyes forward. She should never look down at her feet while carrying on her head; that collapses the neck curve.
- **Weight must be minimal.** For a child her age, this should mean almost nothing—perhaps a dry container for practice, or a very light bundle. Water is deceptively heavy; even a few liters can exceed what her cervical spine should bear.
- **No twisting.** Turn the whole body, not the neck, when changing direction.
- **Frequent breaks.** Set the load down every few minutes if possible.

### Watch for danger signs

Seek medical help if you can, or at minimum stop all carrying, if you notice:
- Clicking, grinding, or catching in the neck
- Headaches after carrying
- Numbness, tingling, or weakness in arms or hands
- She begins to hold her head tilted to one side, or develops a forward-jutting posture
- Pain that persists after resting

### A practical suggestion for the journey

Since you travel before full light, let her job be “navigator” rather than porter. Children remember routes very well when they are not preoccupied with pain or balance. Give her the task of remembering the turn at a certain tree or rock. That builds the skill you want her to have—self-sufficiency and knowledge of the path—without the cost to her growing body.

If your circumstances allow any other option—community help, closer safe water, a cart, or a smaller daily ration carried in a backpack—her neck will be better for it. She has many years ahead to be strong. Right now, your job is to make sure she reaches those years without a chronic neck or spine injury.
